sandhi.note: Visarga before t becomes s. The same change gives अतस्त्वां.
-aḥ before a becomes -o and the following a is elided (avagraha): यतोऽतः. Then अतः before t becomes अतस्.
After a vowel other than a/ā (here ai), the visarga appears as r before a vowel and before a voiced consonant.
Final m joins the vowel of इत्थम्; the m of इत्थम् becomes anusvāra before p.

morph.note: Causative (णिच्) of √कृ, कारयति ‘makes (someone) do’, in the passive participle. In the passive of a causative the person made to act becomes the subject (विष्णुः, अहम्, ईशानः) and the thing done stays accusative (शरीरग्रहणम्). The plural masculine covers all three.

The enclitic ते is formally genitive or dative singular of युष्मद्. Purāṇic and epic verse use it with past participles for the agent, ‘by you’; a genitive of the agent with the participle is the grammatical explanation. Reading ते as the plural pronoun ‘they (were made)’ is also possible, but it sits awkwardly with अहम्.
Optative of possibility in a rhetorical question: कः … शक्तिमान् भवेत् ‘who could be able?’
Possessive -मत् on शक्ति; nom. sg. masculine -मान्. The word echoes शक्तिः of 1.83: she is the शक्ति of all, so who is शक्तिमान् to praise her?

mantras.anvaya: (विष्णुः अहम् ईशानः च शरीरग्रहणं) ते यतः कारिताः, अतः त्वां स्तोतुं कः शक्तिमान् भवेत्? (हे) देवि, सा त्वम् इत्थं स्वैः उदारैः प्रभावैः संस्तुता —
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line completes the sentence begun in 1.84 with a यतः … अतः (‘since … therefore’) pair. The second line opens a new sentence: सा त्वम् … संस्तुता is the subject of the imperatives in 1.86.
mantras.lit: since (we) have been made by you (to take bodies), therefore who could be able to praise you? You, (such as you are), thus praised, O Devī, by (the telling of) your own exalted powers,
mantras.tr: have been made by you to take on bodily form — so who could have the power to praise you? O Devī, praised in this way for your own exalted powers,
mantras.tr_note: The first half finishes 1.84; the second half begins the request that 1.86 states.

comm.t: Brahmā ends the praise with its reason: the three gods owe even their bodies to her, so none of them can praise her adequately. The second line turns from praise to petition: ‘you, thus praised …’ leads straight into the request of 1.86.

The hymn closes in the classical manner of a stotra: an admission that praise falls short, then the request. Here the praise has been nothing but a recital of her own powers (प्रभावैः स्वैः) — she is praised with what is already hers.
A modern reflection: Brahmā asks only after acknowledging what he is. The order — recognition first, request second — is the shape of the whole hymn.

morph.note: Causative stem मोहय- (√मुह् with guṇa + णिच्): ‘cause to be bewildered’. The same root gives महामोहा (1.78) and मोह in the king’s question (1.44) and Medhas’s answer (1.53, 1.55).
Passive imperative: नी + -य- + ātmanepada ending -ताम्. With नी the person led becomes the subject (अच्युतः) and the destination stays accusative (प्रबोधम्).
दुर्- ‘hard to’ with the action noun of आ + √धृष् ‘to assail’: ‘hard to attack’. Grammarians form such words with a special kṛt affix after दुर्, सु and ईषत्.

mantras.anvaya: (हे देवि) एतौ दुराधर्षौ असुरौ मधुकैटभौ मोहय। जगत्स्वामी अच्युतः च लघु प्रबोधं नीयताम्।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two requests: an active imperative to the Goddess (मोहय) and a passive imperative about Viṣṇu (नीयताम्), joined by च.
mantras.lit: delude these two hard-to-assail asuras, Madhu and Kaiṭabha; and let Acyuta, lord of the world, be brought quickly to waking,
mantras.tr: bewilder these two invincible asuras, Madhu and Kaiṭabha, and let Acyuta, the lord of the world, be woken quickly,

comm.t: The request at last: two things, one for each side. Delude the asuras; wake Viṣṇu. Both are acts of the same power — the Goddess as Mahāmāyā clouds the asuras’ minds and, as Yoganidrā, releases the god.

The dhyāna of Mahākālī in the Gita Press pāṭha sums up this scene: she is the one whom the lotus-born (Brahmā) praised, when Hari slept, for the slaying of Madhu and Kaiṭabha (यामस्तौत्स्वपिते हरौ कमलजो हन्तुं मधुं कैटभम्). The dhyāna is liturgical, but it is drawn from these verses.
A modern reflection: the same power is asked both to confuse and to awaken. The text does not treat illusion and clarity as the work of rival powers.

samasa.sense: the two mighty asuras; महत् takes the form महा- as the first member of a karmadhāraya, and महा + असुर gives महासुर (अकः सवर्णे दीर्घः, 6.1.101)

morph.note: Passive imperative of √कृ: the root takes the form क्रि- before the passive -य- (क्रियते ‘is done’), with the ending -ताम्.
Infinitive of purpose: ‘(so that he may) kill’. The objects एतौ महासुरौ are accusative, governed by the infinitive.

mantras.anvaya: अस्य बोधः च एतौ महासुरौ हन्तुं क्रियताम्।
mantras.anvaya_en: A second passive imperative, parallel to नीयताम् in 1.86, with an infinitive of purpose.
mantras.lit: and let his awareness be made, to kill these two great asuras.
mantras.tr: and let him be roused to slay these two great asuras.
mantras.tr_note: बोधः क्रियताम् (‘let awareness be made’) is rendered ‘let him be roused’.

comm.t: The last line of Brahmā’s hymn repeats the second request with a purpose added: wake him so that he may kill the two. प्रबोध (1.86) and बोध here may simply be the same waking said twice, or बोध may mean awareness — knowing what must be done; the text does not decide.

The hymn of Brahmā (1.73–87) is the first of the four great hymns of the Devī Māhātmya; the others come in chapters 4, 5 and 11. In the Śākta tradition it is recited as a hymn to the Goddess as Yoganidrā, the sleep of Viṣṇu.
A modern reflection: the hymn ends with a practical request. Its long praise serves an urgent need, and it says so plainly.

morph.note: Taddhita in -अ with vṛddhi of the first vowel (तमस् → तामस ‘belonging to tamas’); the feminine takes -ई. Tamas is darkness, inertia — the quality of sleep.
Instrumental of वेधस् ‘disposer, ordainer’, an old name of Brahmā; s-stems keep the s before vowel endings (वेधसा, वेधसः).

mantras.anvaya: एवं तदा तत्र वेधसा स्तुता तामसी देवी —
mantras.anvaya_en: The subject with its participle and agent; the main verbs (निर्गम्य … तस्थौ) come in 1.90–91.
mantras.lit: Thus praised then there by Vedhas, the Devī Tāmasī —
mantras.tr: Praised in this way by Brahmā, the Ordainer, the Goddess who is the dark power of sleep
mantras.tr_note: तामसी ‘of tamas’ is rendered ‘the dark power of sleep’ because in this scene she is Viṣṇu’s Yoganidrā (1.66, 1.69); the sentence runs on to 1.91.

comm.t: The hymn has its effect. Medhas names the Goddess here तामसी, ‘of tamas’: she is the dark, heavy power of sleep that holds Viṣṇu, the Yoganidrā Brahmā has just praised.

The Gita Press pāṭha assigns the first carita to Mahākālī as presiding deity (its viniyoga and dhyāna); that assignment is liturgical tradition. तामसी is the word in the Purāṇa’s own text that the assignment most naturally connects with: the first manifestation is the Goddess under the guṇa of tamas.
